elements.quote: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we examined the evidence on transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) as a bridge to elective and emergency surgery in cirrhotic patients.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly identifies the report as a systematic review (and meta-analysis).

elements.quote: We aimed to assess the perioperative characteristics, management approaches, and outcomes of this intervention, which is used to achieve portal decompression and enable the safe performance of elective and emergent surgery.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective of the review.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and Scopus were searched for studies reporting the outcomes of cirrhotic patients undergoing elective and emergency surgery with preoperative TIPS.
elements.reason: The abstract conveys the population/intervention scope (cirrhotic patients, preoperative TIPS, elective/emergency surgery), but no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria (e.g., study designs, comparators) are stated.

elements.quote: MEDLINE and Scopus were searched for studies reporting the outcomes of cirrhotic patients undergoing elective and emergency surgery with preoperative TIPS.
elements.reason: The abstract names the information sources (MEDLINE, Scopus) but does not report when each source was last searched; the search date appears only in the main text (text_12).

elements.quote: The risk of bias was evaluated using the methodological index for non-randomized studies of interventions, and the JBI critical appraisal tool for case reports.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the risk of bias assessment methods (MINORS and JBI tools).

elements.quote: A DerSimonian and Laird (random-effects) model was used to perform the meta-analyses in which the overall (combined) effect estimate was presented in the form of an odds ratio (summary statistic).
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the synthesis methods (random-effects meta-analysis, odds ratios).

elements.quote: Of 426 patients (from 27 articles), 256 (60.1%) underwent preoperative TIPS.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the number of included articles (27) and patients (426) with relevant characteristics (TIPS vs no TIPS).

elements.quote: Random effects MA showed significantly lower odds of postoperative ascites with preoperative TIPS (OR = 0.40, 95% CI 0.22-0.72; I2 = 0%). There were no significant differences in 90-day mortality (3 studies: OR = 0.76, 95% CI 0.33-1.77...)
elements.reason: The abstract reports results for main outcomes (ascites, mortality, transfusions, hepatic encephalopathy, ACLF) with study counts per outcome.
A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals.

elements.quote: significantly lower odds of postoperative ascites with preoperative TIPS
elements.reason: Groups are compared (preoperative TIPS vs non-TIPS) and the direction of effect and favored group are indicated (lower odds of ascites with TIPS; no differences for other outcomes).
The abstract does not mention limitations of the included evidence (e.g., observational data, risk of bias, heterogeneity); limitations appear only in the Discussion (text_22).

elements.quote: Preoperative TIPS appears safe in cirrhotic patients who undergo elective and emergency surgery and may have a potential role in postoperative ascites control. Future randomized clinical trials should test these preliminary results.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation of the results and their implications for future research.
The abstract does not state any funding source for the review.
The abstract provides no registration name or number; the main text (text_5) notes the review was not registered in PROSPERO, but this is not stated in the abstract.

elements.quote: To date, the role of TIPS in the preoperative setting of patients requiring elective and emergency surgery remains unclear. Moreover, little quantitative evidence is available to know the number of patients who can undergo surgery after preoperative TIPS and their associated postoperative outcomes; for example, postoperative liver-related events (LRE).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes the current state of knowledge and key uncertainties regarding preoperative TIPS.

elements.quote: little quantitative evidence is available to know the number of patients who can undergo surgery after preoperative TIPS and their associated postoperative outcomes
elements.reason: The need for the review is implied through the identified evidence gap, but the importance of conducting the review is not explicitly elaborated in the retrieved evidence.

No similar or previous systematic reviews on this topic are cited or mentioned anywhere in the retrieved evidence, so there is no indication that an update or replication of a prior review is being conducted.

elements.quote: which is used to achieve portal decompression and enable the safe performance of elective and emergent surgery
elements.reason: The abstract briefly describes the proposed mechanism of action of TIPS (portal decompression enabling safe surgery).
No logic model or description of hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we examined the evidence on transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) as a bridge to elective and emergency surgery in cirrhotic patients. We aimed to assess the perioperative characteristics, management approaches, and outcomes of this intervention
elements.reason: The review objective is explicitly stated in the abstract ('We aimed to assess...'), but it is not formulated using an explicit question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO), so the element is only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: The outcomes of interest were: 1. Surgery after TIPS; 2. Mortality; 3. Perioperative transfusions; and 4. Postoperative liver-related events.
elements.reason: The population (cirrhotic patients undergoing elective and emergency surgery), intervention (preoperative TIPS), and outcomes are stated, and the comparison (TIPS vs non-TIPS) is implied in the meta-analysis description (text_14), but the planned comparisons are not explicitly presented in a formal PICO-style statement.

elements.quote: Studies were considered eligible for inclusion if they reported the characteristics and outcomes of cirrhotic patients undergoing elective and emergency surgery with preoperative TIPS.
elements.reason: Population, intervention, and setting are specified; text_8 additionally specifies eligible designs: 'We included observational studies of any type (case series, cohort studies, case-control studies). Case reports were also considered eligible'.
No reporting of restrictions by publication year, language, or publication status in the retrieved evidence.
The evidence does not indicate exclusion of studies based on outcome measurement vs reporting; no distinction is applicable based on retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: a DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis was performed to assess the overall outcomes of TIPS compared to non-TIPS groups
elements.reason: The synthesis groups (TIPS vs non-TIPS) are specified for the meta-analysis, but grouping for the broader synthesis of non-comparative studies (case series, case reports) is not explicitly defined or linked to the review objectives.

elements.quote: Studies on cirrhotic patients undergoing hepatic surgery (i.e., hepatic resection or liver transplantation) and those involving subjects with non-cirrhotic portal hypertension were excluded.
elements.reason: Restrictions on hepatic surgery and non-cirrhotic portal hypertension are stated but no rationale is provided for these exclusions.

We intended to collect data on the following postoperative LREs (if available from primary studies): ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, portal hypertensive bleeding and acute on chronic liver failure (ACLF).

elements.quote: We also registered the timeframe from TIPS to surgery and if the surgical procedure was elective or emergent.

elements.quote: We intended to collect data on the following postoperative LREs (if available from primary studies): ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, portal hypertensive bleeding and acute on chronic liver failure (ACLF).

elements.quote: For case series and comparative studies, we used the methodological index for non-randomized studies (MINORS) tool to assess their quality and internal validity [13]. ... The methodological quality of case reports was critically appraised through the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tool for case reports.
elements.reason: Both tools (MINORS and JBI case report tool) are named.

elements.quote: MINORS critically appraises non-randomized studies across eight methodological domains in cases of observational studies without a comparison group (i.e., case series). For comparative studies, four additional items are evaluated. Each item in the MINORS tool was scored as 0: if not reported (Red: high risk of bias); 1: reported but inadequate (Yellow: unclear risk of bias); and 2: reported and adequate (Green: low risk of bias).
elements.reason: Domains/items and scoring of MINORS are described; JBI tool items are not detailed but the main tool's components are specified.

elements.quote: Each item in the MINORS tool was scored as 0: if not reported (Red: high risk of bias); 1: reported but inadequate (Yellow: unclear risk of bias); and 2: reported and adequate (Green: low risk of bias).
elements.reason: Item-level scoring mapped to risk-of-bias categories is given, but explicit rules for deriving an overall judgement are not reported.
No adaptations to existing tools are described.
Only existing tools (MINORS, JBI) were used; no new tool was developed.

No evidence of contacting investigators for risk-of-bias information; process not described.
No automation tools for risk-of-bias assessment were reported or implied.

elements.quote: A DerSimonian and Laird (random-effects) model was used to perform the meta-analyses in which the overall (combined) effect estimate was presented in the form of an odds ratio (summary statistic).
elements.reason: The effect measure (odds ratio) used for the meta-analyzed outcomes is explicitly specified, and results are consistently reported as ORs for each outcome (ascites, mortality, transfusions, hepatic encephalopathy, ACLF).
No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect sizes (e.g., what OR magnitude is considered clinically meaningful) are reported anywhere in the retrieved evidence.
No methods for re-expressing synthesized results using another effect measure are described; only 2x2 table-derived odds ratios are used.
The choice of the odds ratio as effect measure is stated but no justification for this choice is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: When available, we extracted data from comparative studies on the outcomes of interest: mortality and LREs. First, the number of individuals who did and did not experience the outcome in the treatment and control groups of each study was extracted into a 2 × 2 table. Then, a DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis was performed to assess the overall outcomes of TIPS compared to non-TIPS groups.
elements.reason: The Data Synthesis section partially describes the decision process for synthesis eligibility: only comparative studies with available data on the prespecified outcomes (mortality, LREs) extractable into 2×2 tables entered the meta-analysis, and a rule selected the publication with the larger sample size or greater granularity when populations overlapped. The Results (text_15) add that 'four were comparative studies, of which three were evaluated as appropriate to combine in meta-analyses [19, 37, 40]'. However, the manuscript does not describe the actual criteria or process used to judge the studies 'appropriate to combine' (e.g., tabulating study/intervention characteristics and comparing them against the planned synthesis groups), nor why the fourth comparative study was not meta-analyzed, so the description of processes for deciding eligibility for each synthesis is incomplete.

elements.quote: First, the number of individuals who did and did not experience the outcome in the treatment and control groups of each study was extracted into a 2 × 2 table. ... When two articles appeared to be reporting data from overlapping populations (i.e., different papers reporting data from the same population or the exact center/hospital during overlapping periods), the publication with the larger sample size or greater/deepest data granularity was selected for inclusion.
elements.reason: The Data Synthesis section describes some data preparation steps for synthesis: converting extracted outcome counts into 2×2 tables prior to the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects meta-analysis, and a rule for handling overlapping publications (selecting the report with larger sample size or deepest granularity). However, methods for handling missing summary statistics (e.g., imputation, contacting authors, conversions such as median-to-mean) are not described; the phrase 'When available, we extracted data' only implies missing data without explaining how unavailability was managed, so the data-preparation description is incomplete.

elements.quote: All analyses were performed in Stata statistical software.
elements.reason: Software (Stata) is named, but no version number is reported.

elements.quote: The information collected from each study was summarized descriptively to chart the available literature.
elements.reason: Descriptive synthesis is described for studies not suitable for meta-analysis.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity was evaluated using the I 2 test. An I 2 > 75% revealed high heterogeneity.
